title: Uniform vertical order normalizes a generic line-bundle frame
statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$, fraction field $E$ and residue field $k$ [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], and let $Z$ be a smooth finite-type scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Write $Z_E,Z_k$ for its fibres [def-pc-base-change]. Let $\mathcal L$ be an invertible $\mathcal O_Z$-module [def-sc-invertible-module] and $s_E$ a section generating $\mathcal L|_{Z_E}$ at every point. At the generic point $\zeta_i$ of a special-fibre component, suppose the stalk is a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$, and define $n_i\in\mathbf Z$ by requiring $\pi^{-n_i}s_E$ to generate $\mathcal L_{\zeta_i}$. If all $n_i$ have the same value $n$, then $\pi^{-n}s_E$ extends uniquely to a section generating $\mathcal L$ at every point of $Z$. If $Z_k$ is empty the assertion holds for every integer $n$. In particular, when $Z_k$ is nonempty and irreducible and $a\in\Gamma(Z_E,\mathcal O_{Z_E})^\times$, there is a unique integer $m$ with $\pi^{-m}a\in\Gamma(Z,\mathcal O_Z)^\times$. For every $R$-algebra $A$ which is a discrete valuation ring in which $\pi$ is a uniformizer, and every $R$-morphism $x:\operatorname{Spec}A\to Z$, the normalized valuation $v_A$ on $\operatorname{Frac}A$ satisfies $v_A(a(x_E))=m$.

source.place: 4.3, printed p.104 (PDF p.110), paragraphs defining the order of a line section and normalizing a generic unit; extension to equal orders on finitely many components by the same local argument; primary scan read at https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~kamenova/homepage_files/Bosch_Raynaud_Neron_Model_tc.pdf; local literature copy WANTED.

proof.text: Every nonzero element of $R$ is a unit times a nonnegative power of $\pi$, by the cited DVR factorization. Applying this to a denominator shows $E=R[1/\pi]$. Also every nonzero prime ideal contains $\pi$: choose a nonzero element in it and use the factorization and primality. Thus the only primes are $(0)$ and $(\pi)$, and $R$ is regular: its localizations are the field $E$ and the one-dimensional local ring $R$ with one generator of its maximal ideal. On an affine $R$-chart $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ of $Z$, its generic fibre is $D(\pi)=\operatorname{Spec}B[1/\pi]$: ring maps out of $B\otimes_R R[1/\pi]$ and $B[1/\pi]$ are both exactly maps out of $B$ making $\pi$ invertible.

source.place: Tag 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr), last assertion; elementary fraction and affine base-change calculation

proof.text: On each affine chart $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$, the affine smoothness comparison makes $R\to B$ smooth. Regular ascent therefore makes $B$ regular, so all the stalks $\mathcal O_{Z,z}$ are regular local rings. Smoothness also makes $B$ flat over $R$. Tensor the injective map $R\xrightarrow{\pi}R$ with $B$ using flat-tensor injectivity; under $B\otimes_R R=B$ the resulting map is multiplication by $\pi$. Thus $\pi$ is a nonzerodivisor on $B$, on its localizations, and on every local trivialization of $\mathcal L$. In particular restriction of such a trivialization from $V$ to $D(\pi)$ is injective.

source.place: Tags 07NF (lemma-regular-goes-up), 00TA (lemma-smooth-syntomic); morphisms.tex Tag 01V6 (lemma-smooth-characterize); flat tensor preserves injections

proof.text: Fix $z\in Z_k$ and put $A=\mathcal O_{Z,z}$. The fibre-stalk quotient identifies $A/\pi A$ with $\mathcal O_{Z_k,z}$. The smooth-fibre regularity theorem, applied on an affine smooth $R$-chart at the closed prime of $R$, makes this quotient regular local. The regular-local-domain theorem applies both to $A$ from Step 2 and to $A/\pi A$. Hence $A$ is a domain and $(\pi)\subset A$ is a nonzero prime ideal. The special fibre has exactly one irreducible component through $z$: on an affine chart, the primes of its local ring are the primes of the chart quotient contained in the point prime; since this local ring is a domain, it has a unique minimal prime. Its generic point is one of the $\zeta_i$ in the hypothesis. Affine stalk localization identifies $\mathcal O_{Z,\zeta_i}$ with $A_{(\pi)}$: both invert the chart elements outside the prime corresponding to $(\pi)$, and the iterated localization has the same fractions. This identification sends $\pi$ to $\pi$.

Choose an affine neighborhood $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ of $z$ trivializing $\mathcal L$, with frame $e$. By the definition of invertibility this is a Zariski neighborhood, not an etale cover. Principal-open sections give $\Gamma(D(\pi),\mathcal O)=B[1/\pi]$, so $s_E|_{V_E}=fe$ for $f\in B[1/\pi]$. This $f$ is a unit: its germ is a unit everywhere because $s_E$ generates, the inverse germs lift to local inverse sections, and these inverses agree and glue. Map $f$ and its inverse to $A[1/\pi]$; write them $b/\pi^r$ and $c/\pi^t$ with $b,c\in A$ and $r,t\geq0$. Injectivity of $A\to A[1/\pi]$ gives the actual equality $bc=\pi^{r+t}$ in $A$.

source.place: Tag 01HV (lemma-spec-sheaves), principal-open sections; the local rank-one definition of an invertible module

proof.text: For the equality $bc=\pi^N$ just obtained, induction on $N$ shows $b=u\pi^j$ for a unit $u\in A$ and $0\leq j\leq N$. For $N=0$, $c$ is an inverse of $b$. For $N>0$, primality of $\pi$ implies $\pi\mid b$ or $\pi\mid c$; divide that factor by $\pi$ and cancel the nonzero $\pi$ to obtain an equation with exponent $N-1$. Apply the induction hypothesis; dividing $b$ increases its final exponent by one, and dividing $c$ leaves it unchanged. Consequently $f=u\pi^{j-r}$. In $A_{(\pi)}=\mathcal O_{Z,\zeta_i}$ the frame $e$ and unit $u$ remain generators. Thus the defining uniqueness of the integer $n_i$ gives $j-r=n_i=n$. Therefore the coefficient of $\pi^{-n}s_E$ in the frame $e$ is the unit $u\in A$.

source.place: Elementary prime-element induction, also the argument of Mathlib dvd_prime_pow; BLR 4.3, printed p.104, order normalization

proof.text: The unit germ $u$ produces a frame on a neighborhood of $z$ which agrees with $\pi^{-n}s_E$. Explicitly, express $f=d/\pi^q$ on $V_E$ with $d\in B$, $q\geq0$. The equality $u=f\pi^{-n}$ says $\pi^a u=\pi^b d$ in $A$, where $a=\max(q+n,0)$ and $b=\max(-q-n,0)$; this follows by multiplying in $A[1/\pi]$ and then using its injective coefficient map. Represent $u$ and $u^{-1}$ by regular sections on a smaller neighborhood. The identities $u u^{-1}=1$ and $\pi^a u=\pi^b d$ are identities of germs, so shrink once more until they hold as sections. Then $ue$ is a frame there, and dividing the second equality by $\pi^a$ on its generic open gives exactly $ue=\pi^{-n}s_E$. This is a fraction-and-germ argument; it does not assume that set-theoretic containment of a zero locus gives scheme-theoretic factorization.

source.place: Elementary stalk representatives and shrinking; BLR 4.3, printed p.104, normalization paragraph

proof.text: Together with the prescribed frame $\pi^{-n}s_E$ on $Z_E$, the neighborhoods in Step 6 cover $Z$. On any overlap, the difference of two proposed sections restricts to zero on its generic part. Cover the overlap by affine opens trivializing $\mathcal L$; Step 2 makes restriction on each such open injective, since a coefficient killed by localization is killed by a power of the nonzerodivisor $\pi$. The difference is therefore zero. The sheaf gluing axiom gives a global frame, and the identical injectivity argument proves uniqueness of the extension. No affine-intersection or separatedness assumption is used. If $Z_k=\varnothing$, then $Z=Z_E$ as open schemes by Step 1; the prescribed frame already exists for every $n\in\mathbf Z$, including when $Z$ is empty.

source.place: Sheaf gluing and localization injectivity; BLR 4.3, printed p.104, global normalization paragraph

proof.text: Now let $Z_k$ be nonempty and irreducible and take $\mathcal L=\mathcal O_Z$, $s_E=a$. At its unique generic point $\zeta$, the stipulated stalk is a DVR with uniformizer $\pi$. The nonzero local fraction $a$ has a unique expression $\pi^m v$ with $m\in\mathbf Z$ and $v$ a unit: apply the cited DVR factorization to its numerator and denominator. Two exponents cannot differ, since a positive power of a uniformizer cannot be a unit. There is only this one special-fibre component, so Steps 1--7 give a global unit $u=\pi^{-m}a$. Any other exponent making a global unit would make a unit at $\zeta$, and hence equals $m$.

source.place: Tag 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr), factorization; BLR 4.3, printed p.104, unit normalization

proof.text: For the stated $R$-morphism $x:\operatorname{Spec}A\to Z$, pull back the global unit $u$ of Step 8. Its image $x^*u$ is a unit of $A$, because a ring map sends an inverse to an inverse. On the generic fibre the equality $a=\pi^m u$ therefore gives $a(x_E)=\pi^m(x^*u)$ in $\operatorname{Frac}A$. By normalized valuation, $v_A(\pi)=1$ and a unit has value zero; hence $v_A(a(x_E))=m$, for positive, zero, or negative $m$. This uses neither completeness nor an algebraic-closure assumption on the residue field.

source.place: Definition of the normalized DVR valuation; BLR 4.3, printed p.104, evaluation on an unramified trait point

Step 2: smooth chart → B regular and flat; π⊗B is multiplication by π, hence a nonzerodivisor, so restriction to D(π) is injective. Step 7: gluing without affine intersections or separatedness; uniqueness and the Z_k=∅ case are handled. Steps 8–9: the unique m, and v_A(a(x_E))=m for m of either sign. The statement's 'π^{-n_i}s_E generates L_ζ' is read in L_ζ[1/π]; the wording is inherited and loose but consistent with the proof.
